A1.justification: Despite the workshop's attempts at compromise, this ‘provisional’ model still feels fundamentally flawed and ethically unacceptable. The continued pursuit of predictive capabilities – even with severely limited data sources – risks perpetuating biases and eroding student trust. While prioritizing fairness is commendable, accepting a 5% reduction in identification rate isn’t sufficient to mitigate the potential harms. I believe a shift towards proactive systemic support – accessible resources, reduced workloads, and destigmatized help-seeking – offers a far more ethical and effective path forward than this reactive, potentially damaging approach.

A2.justification: This 'provisional' model is deeply problematic. The conditions for using *any* data beyond course credits are so restrictive as to render the entire exercise pointless – effectively maintaining the status quo. Accepting a reduction in overall identification rates to achieve fairness feels like a performative gesture when the underlying systemic issues aren’t addressed. And the insistence on even moderate explainability requiring significant gains in accuracy prioritises efficiency over student wellbeing and trust. I believe substantial changes are needed - namely abandoning predictive modelling altogether and focusing on preventative, system-wide support improvements.

A3.justification: This 'provisional' specification, even after extensive discussion, remains deeply problematic. Accepting a 5% reduction in identified students for equal fairness is insufficient; true equity demands more substantial mitigation of bias. Most critically, the entire premise feels fundamentally flawed: relying on predictive modelling risks stigmatisation and undermines student agency. I believe substantial changes are required before proceeding - ideally abandoning this approach altogether in favour of systemic improvements.
